title: Weekly Briefing: The Middle Manager Purge, Home Depot’s 40-Year Career Ladder, and Why Workers Would Take a Pay Cut for Job Security 2026
author: Jacob Morgan
source: Future Ready Leadership With Jacob Morgan (greatleadership.substack.com), September 21,
summary: Jacob Morgan's weekly briefing comments on three workplace stories linked by how people think about stability, growth and leadership. On the Wall Street Journal's report of companies stripping out middle managers, he distinguishes cutting bureaucracy from assuming management itself is unnecessary, noting a projected shortage of 2.9 million managers by 2032. On Fortune's profile of Ann-Marie Campbell's rise from a $4.15-an-hour Home Depot cashier to senior executive, he argues that long careers require visible internal ladders. On a MarketWatch report that most workers would trade pay for job security, he concludes that stability has rejoined the employee value proposition. He ties the three together by arguing that aggressive restructuring creates the very uncertainty that good managers help employees navigate.
points: Morgan argues good middle managers translate strategy into execution and absorb friction between senior leaders and the front line, work AI does not remove.
Companies that remove management layers now may find strong managers scarce when they need them again.
Internal mobility is framed as the clearest signal that growth is actually possible inside a company.
With 54 percent of surveyed workers willing to accept a pay cut for security, leaders who offer clarity about the future offer something scarce.
quotes: There is nothing inherently wrong with flattening an organization. Plenty of companies have too many layers and too many people whose days are consumed by meetings, approvals, and passing information from one level to another. But there is a big difference between removing unnecessary bureaucracy and assuming middle management itself is unnecessary.

Good middle managers translate executive strategy into something teams can actually execute. They coach employees, resolve conflict, notice when someone is struggling, and often absorb the friction between senior leadership and the front line.
The better question is not whether companies should have fewer managers. It is which managers are creating real value and which layers simply create friction.
The lesson for employers is just as important. You cannot ask people to build long careers with you if there is nowhere for them to go.
Internal mobility is not just an HR program. It is one of the clearest signals that growth is actually possible inside the company.
This does not mean companies should start paying people less. It means stability has become part of the employee value proposition again.
When organizations flatten aggressively and restructure constantly, employees do not experience that as an abstract efficiency exercise. They experience it as uncertainty about their own future.
